strengths: Practical efficiency improvements: Achieves 20-60% latency reduction and 35% memory savings while maintaining accuracy comparable to dense attention on Needle-in-Haystack and LongBench
Data-driven approach without retraining: Dynamically predicts sparsity patterns without manual specification or base model retraining, providing genuine adaptability across tasks

Comprehensive technical presentation: Extensive implementation details in appendix, clear algorithms, good visualizations (especially Figure 5 comparing dynamic vs static chunking), and honest limitations discussion

Thoughtful engineering choices: Length-normalized aggregation for variable-length chunks, soft labeling with focal BCE loss for class imbalance, NMS for robust boundary detection, and automatic label generation from attention patterns
Strong relative improvements over baselines: Outperforms block sparse attention by 6-18% relative gains on LongBench while maintaining comparable or lower computational cost
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Hierarchical prediction (chunk-level→token-level), boundary detection, and length normalization are relatively straightforward techniques; the contribution is primarily their combination rather than fundamental methodological advances

Incomplete baseline comparisons: Despite introducing several dynamic methods (Minference, LM-Infinite, H2O, Scissorhands) as motivation, only block sparse attention is compared; missing comparisons with key competing approaches

Narrow experimental scope: Only tested on small Gemma models (1-2B parameters) with limited context (max 8k); lacks evaluation on larger models where efficiency gains are more impactful; authors explicitly acknowledge inability to extend context length

Circular dependency in boundary detection: Boundary labels derived from existing model's attention patterns, then predictor trained to replicate those patterns; unclear whether this optimizes for actual sparse attention task performance vs. merely fitting existing patterns

Hyperparameter dependence contradicts 'data-driven' claims: Requires tuning chunk budget, chunk size, window size (w=4), hidden size (256), NMS thresholds, and focal loss weights with limited ablation studies justifying these choices

Accuracy gaps on some tasks: LongBench results show notable deficits (e.g., NrtvQA: 20.69 vs 22.37 dense); DHSA(+bs) variant sometimes performs worse, suggesting method doesn't universally match dense attention

Blank code availability link and limited reproducibility details: Code link not provided; training uses only first 10,000 samples from datasets with limited justification; many hyperparameter choices (w=4, α=2.0) appear arbitrary

Insufficient ablation and failure analysis: No ablations on key design choices like √|C| scaling factor or 5-feature fusion; missing analysis of when dynamic chunking fails or which tasks/domains benefit most from approach

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem of long-context inference efficiency with comprehensive experimental evaluation across Needle-in-a-Haystack and LongBench benchmarks
Plug-in architecture allows integration without base model retraining, with detailed implementation details and pseudocode that aid reproducibility
Dynamic content-aware chunking via learned boundary predictor is a reasonable approach that adapts better than static sparse patterns
Extensive appendix with architecture details, training procedures, and detailed latency/memory analysis across multiple implementation backends
weaknesses: Claims of 'without retraining' are misleading—the boundary predictor requires training on Long Data Collections using accumulated attention patterns from dense attention, creating a circular dependency undermining efficiency arguments

Severely limited experimental scope: only 2b/1b models (no larger models), maximum 8k token context with authors explicitly unable to extend beyond this ('no reliable implementation,' 'unexpected behavior'), limiting practical relevance

Mixed empirical results inconsistent with abstract claims: DHSA underperforms dense attention on multiple LongBench tasks (NarrativeQA: 20.69 vs 22.37, HotpotQA: 38.78 vs 41.63), and 6-18% gains are only versus weak block sparse baseline, missing comparisons with recent dynamic methods like Minference

Insufficient technical justification: length normalization (Eq. 4) choice of √|C| is unexplained with no ablation; simple upsampling mechanism treating all tokens in a chunk uniformly lacks justification; boundary prediction labels are heuristic-based with multiple unjustified hyperparameters

Critical missing ablations and analysis: no component-level ablations isolating contributions of hierarchical structure vs. dynamic chunking; no sensitivity analysis for hyperparameters; no error analysis or failure case discussion; DHSA(+bs) variant sometimes underperforms, indicating unexplored design sensitivity
Reproducibility concerns: code URL missing ('available at .'), hyperparameter guidance for new domains/models unclear, only 10k training samples used with no data requirement analysis

Incremental novelty for ICML: individual components (hierarchical attention, dynamic chunking, boundary detection) are not novel; their combination is a straightforward engineering contribution without theoretical insights or consistent empirical validation

strengths: Well-motivated practical approach with clear efficiency gains (20-60% latency reduction, 35% memory savings) on real benchmarks (Needle-in-a-Haystack, LongBench)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with extensive latency/memory profiling, detailed appendices, and good visualizations of how dynamic chunking adapts better than static patterns
Data-driven method that adapts to input content without retraining base model; thoughtful design choices (length-normalized aggregation, soft labeling, focal loss) with good justification
Honest discussion of limitations and clear scope definition; plug-and-play architecture enhancing practical accessibility
Solid experimental methodology with consistent 6-18% improvements over block sparse attention and accuracy matching dense attention
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: individual components (hierarchical chunking, boundary detection, adaptive aggregation) are not new; contribution is primarily their specific combination

Critical gap in related work: no direct comparison with cited dynamic sparse methods (Minference, H2O, LM-Infinite, Scissorhands)—only compared against block sparse and static methods, undermining claims of improvement over prior dynamic approaches
Severely restricted evaluation scope: only two small models (2B, 1B parameters) tested; no results on 7B+ models or architectures beyond Gemma (LLaMA, Qwen, Mistral, etc.)

Circular dependency in boundary predictor training: uses attention patterns from trained model as ground truth labels, potentially biasing predictor to specific model behavior; generalization to different architectures unclear

Context-length extension failure is problematic: authors acknowledge they could not reliably extend maximum context length on Gemma and this effort was abandoned, contradicting a key stated motivation
No hyperparameter sensitivity analysis despite numerous design choices (window size w, NMS window, soft label params α/β/ζ, boundary threshold θᵣ); unclear how to set these for new domains/models
Missing code link: abstract states code is 'available at .' with blank URL, hindering reproducibility
Missing ablation studies on key components: no validation of length normalization impact, comparison of automatic labeling to alternatives, or analysis of information loss in upsampling
Incomplete analysis of design decisions: decode stage grouping of generated tokens into single chunk is ad-hoc; asymmetric prefill/decode handling lacks thorough justification

strengths: Well-motivated dynamic attention approach that addresses task-dependent sparsity patterns, moving beyond static templates with strong empirical validation across multiple benchmarks (NIAH, LongBench, RULER) and model families.

Technically solid hierarchical routing mechanism combining dynamic boundary detection, length-normalized chunk representations, and practical sparse attention backends that preserves exact causal semantics while reducing complexity from O(L²) to O(L·N_b).

Comprehensive experimental evaluation with fair comparisons against 8 baselines, extensive ablation studies (Table 4) validating each component, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis (Table 7), and multi-model/precision evaluation demonstrating generalization.

Exceptional reproducibility with complete algorithms, implementation details across Sections A-C, training/inference procedures, overhead breakdowns, and detailed baseline configurations; code availability promised.

Strong empirical results: 12-20% relative accuracy gains over Block Sparse at comparable cost, scales to 100K context on single 24GB GPU with 10× speedup, generalizes across LLaMA/Qwen/Gemma families, works on GPU/CPU.

Theoretical analysis (Section B) formalizing why DHSA achieves near-oracle recall (1 - 2δ/m) versus block-sparse's O(m/B) bound under semantic segment assumptions, providing intuitive justification for dynamic chunking.
weaknesses: Scope limited to prefill acceleration only; decoding remains dense attention. This is a fundamental limitation for generation-heavy workloads and long reasoning chains, severely reducing applicability for many real-world scenarios.

Boundary predictor requires per-model-family training (~9 hours each) on QA-oriented datasets (TriviaQA, ChatQA2, Long Data). Generalization to out-of-domain texts (code, technical documents, summarization) is unvalidated despite cross-task claims; no cross-domain evaluation provided.

Batch inference processes examples sequentially via for-loops rather than batched computation, limiting throughput for production serving scenarios. Comparison of batch performance against other sparse methods is missing.

Theoretical analysis makes strong unverified assumptions: ε_intra ≪ Δ_inter may not hold generally; semantic segment definition is informal; assumes equal-length segments despite DHSA using variable-length chunks. Practical relevance limited.

Routing overhead (boundary prediction + chunk selection) is non-negligible: 282ms at 8K tokens, scaling to 944ms at 32K (40% of sparse kernel time at 32K per Table 10). Paper underemphasizes this trade-off.

Critical design choices lack ablation/justification: √L_k scaling in Eq. 4 not compared against alternatives; attention ratio threshold θ_r=1.1 appears arbitrary; feature fusion (Eq. 2) without component ablations; automatic labeling parameters hand-tuned.

Evaluation skews toward QA/retrieval tasks (LongBench) with weak performance on synthetic tasks (45.7 vs 44.2 Block-Sparse). Missing evaluation on generation, reasoning, or code. RULER limited to 48K context. Truncation strategy may bias results.

Batch inference is only faster than dense FA2 due to memory constraints, not algorithmic efficiency. High-throughput scenarios would suffer significantly compared to dense or properly batched sparse attention.

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (NIAH, LongBench, RULER) with 8 baseline comparisons and ablation studies
Solid empirical results achieving near-dense accuracy at 12.5% token density across multiple model families (LLaMA, Qwen, Gemma)
Practical system contributions with dual backends (SDPA + tiled online-softmax) supporting GPU/CPU and multiple model families
Enables 100K context inference on memory-constrained hardware (24GB GPU) where dense attention fails
Theoretical framework (Section B) formalizing when dynamic chunking outperforms fixed block-sparse under semantic segment assumptions
Substantial implementation clarity with detailed algorithms and engineering choices supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty—primarily combines existing techniques (hierarchical chunking, boundary detection, length normalization) without fundamental new insights; main difference vs. Block-Sparse Attention is learned vs. fixed boundaries, which feels incremental

Circular bias in training setup: boundary predictor trained on attention patterns to predict sparse attention; unclear why patterns from QA training data generalize to diverse LongBench tasks (code, synthesis, few-shot)

Unfair experimental comparisons: incomplete baseline coverage (DuoAttention/SeerAttention/Quest omitted for 2/3 models), sequence truncation favoring retrieval structure, batch processing via sequential loops, conflating learned-routing advantage with algorithm quality

Theoretical analysis gaps: core assumptions (B.2-B.3) about semantic segments are stated formally but never empirically validated; Proposition B.5 assumes near-perfect boundary detection (δ ≪ m) but actual accuracy not quantified

Modest empirical gains (12-20% relative improvement over Block-Sparse) do not justify added complexity of per-model training, routing overhead (237-944ms per Table 10), and boundary predictor maintenance
Prefill-only optimization limiting practical impact for generation tasks where decoding typically dominates; Needle-in-a-Haystack is artificial retrieval task not representative of real workloads
Length normalization (Eq. 4) lacks principled justification—√L_k scaling motivated informally without explaining why this is better than alternatives (LayerNorm, learnable pooling)

Per-model-family boundary predictor training required (8.89 hours per model) reduces generality; training data limited to 10K samples per dataset with 100 validation samples raises generalization concerns

Automatic labeling circularity: boundary labels depend on current queries' attention distributions; no evidence labels correlate with semantic structure or generalize across different query distributions
Missing failure case analysis and out-of-distribution evaluation; no evidence QA-trained predictor generalizes to fundamentally different LongBench task types

strengths: Addresses practical and timely problem: efficient long-context inference on memory-constrained hardware with clear real-world impact

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: three benchmarks (NIAH, LongBench, RULER), three model families, eight baselines, fair comparisons with matched token density, extensive ablations and sensitivity analyses
Significant practical results: 12-20% relative accuracy gains over Block-Sparse, 10× prefill speedup at 128K context, enables 100K context on single 24GB GPU

Well-motivated technical contributions: dynamic boundary detection using attention patterns is learned rather than heuristic-based, length-normalized chunk representation cleverly handles variable-length chunks, hierarchical routing reduces complexity from O(L²) to O(L·Nb)
Hardware and model agnostic implementation with multiple backends (GPU SDPA, tiled online-softmax, CPU) across multiple open-weight families
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and thorough appendices including implementation details, theoretical analysis, and complete ablations
Thoughtful engineering: multiple backends, careful shared hyperparameters, memory optimizations for very long sequences, honest discussion of limitations
weaknesses: Boundary predictor trained only on QA-oriented datasets (TriviaQA, ChatQA2) but must generalize to diverse downstream tasks; generalization claim lacks formal justification and direct validation across non-QA domains
Automatic boundary labeling (Eqs. 5-7) is heuristic and not validated; no analysis of label quality, correlation with true semantic boundaries, or sensitivity to labeling scheme

Theoretical analysis (Appendix B) rests on strong unvalidated assumptions: Assumption B.2 (intra-segment homogeneity ≪ inter-segment separation) and Assumption B.3 (boundary accuracy) likely violated in practice; no empirical validation of whether δ ≪ m is achieved
Prefill-only optimization ignores decoding efficiency, which is crucial for many long-context applications with long outputs; acknowledged but limits practical applicability
Limited failure mode analysis: wide variance in task performance (Table 1) not explained; no characterization of attention patterns where DHSA underperforms or what structures it struggles with
Experimental design concerns: LongBench inputs truncated to fit memory, some baselines use different implementations (decoding-focused), token density choices somewhat arbitrary
Batch inference handled suboptimally via for-loop rather than batching; Figure 9 shows speedup degrades with batch size, potentially limiting throughput in production settings
Moderate novelty: combines existing techniques (sparse attention, hierarchical routing) in effective but incremental way; no fundamental algorithmic innovations
